title: Group Safari Payments, Rooming Lists and Free Places, Sorted Before Anyone Flies
meta_title: Group Safari Payments and Rooming Lists Explained
meta_description: Group safari payments made simple: deposits, split payments, free places and rooming lists for organisers planning safaris in Kenya and East Africa.
excerpt: Group safari payments, rooming lists and free places explained for organisers, from the 30 to 40% deposit to who shares which tent.
content:
Group safari payments run most smoothly when each traveller pays their own share in two stages: a 30 to 40% deposit, then the balance 2 to 4 weeks before travel. On our group bookings the seventh place is free for every six paying travellers, and you can see how we organise group safaris from first enquiry to final transfer.

The money is rarely the hard part. What wears organisers down is chasing twenty people for passport details, working out who shares a tent with whom and deciding what happens when one person pulls out a month before a Kenya safari or a gorilla trek. This guide to group safari payments and rooms shares the systems we use in our Nairobi office, with tables you can copy.

Quick Facts

  • Deposit: 30 to 40% of each traveller's share holds the booking
  • Balance: Due 2 to 4 weeks before travel
  • Free places: The seventh place is free for every six paying travellers
  • Who pays: Group safari payments can be split by traveller or made by one payer
  • Flights: Members can arrive on different flights and dates
  • Rooms: Mostly doubles and twins; triples and singles are limited at camps
  • Countries: Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda, Namibia and Botswana

How Do Group Safari Payments Work?

Group safari payments follow a simple pattern: a deposit secures lodges, vehicles and permits, and the balance follows shortly before departure. With Divulge Adventures the deposit is 30 to 40% and the balance falls 2 to 4 weeks before travel, and each person can pay directly.

The deposit matters more than it looks. Lodges hold group rooms only for a short time, and gorilla permits are sold in fixed daily numbers. Once group safari payments for the deposit land, we confirm rooms and book permits in each traveller's name, and the trip becomes a booking.

One payer or everyone paying separately?

Families and companies often pay as one, because a single invoice suits a finance team or grandparents treating everyone. Clubs, friends and church parties usually prefer split group safari payments, so every member pays us directly and gets their own receipt. Nobody has to hold other people's money, and one late payer does not freeze the booking for the rest.

If you do collect money yourself, keep a ledger of each name, amount, date and reference. Transfers from abroad and card payments can carry bank charges, so check fees before you choose a method.

StageWhenWhat it secures
Enquiry and quoteAs early as possible; 6 to 12 months for peak monthsA draft route, room plan and per-person price
Deposit (30 to 40%)When the group confirmsLodge rooms, vehicles and permit bookings
Names and passportsWith the depositPermits and internal flights in each traveller's name
Rooming listAbout 6 to 8 weeks before travelFinal room types at every lodge
Balance2 to 4 weeks before travelFinal confirmation of every service

Our article on what a group safari costs per person explains how the price per head falls as vehicles fill.

Who Gets the Free Place, and How Is It Shared?

The free place belongs to the group, and the group decides who uses it. On our group bookings the seventh place is free for every six paying travellers, so a party of 14 has two free places. Settle the rule before any group safari payments are made, because changing it later causes arguments.

Many groups give the free place to the organiser, who often spends dozens of unpaid hours on the trip. Schools and youth groups give it to a teacher or chaperone. Clubs of friends sometimes ask us to spread the saving across every paying member.

Ask what the free place includes before you promise it to anyone. International flights are always paid separately, and fixed government charges such as gorilla permits may be treated differently from lodge and vehicle costs. We set out exactly what the free place covers in each group quote, so nobody is surprised at balance time.

Free places and group safari payments when numbers change

If your group of 14 drops to 12, you lose one free place, and the paying members carry a little more of the shared cost. Tell everyone this at the start. It is also a good reason to hold a short waiting list, because a new traveller who joins before the rooming list closes keeps the maths in your favour.

How Do You Build a Safari Rooming List?

A safari rooming list is a single table that shows every room, who sleeps in it and the bed type, for every night of the trip. Lodges use it to allocate rooms and tents. It changes often, so keep one version and date it.

Start by asking every traveller three questions on one form: who they will share with, whether they need a double or twin beds, and whether they would rather pay extra for a room alone. Add diets, allergies and mobility needs, and keep the form next to your payment ledger so you can see who is confirmed.

Room typeSleepsWhat organisers should know
Double2 in one bedCouples; ask lodges early in busy months
Twin2 in two bedsFriends and colleagues; the usual group choice
Triple or family room3 or moreLimited at tented camps; book first
Single1Usually carries a single supplement

Single rooms and group safari payments

Single supplements are the part of group safari payments that most often feel unfair, so be clear about them. A traveller who wants a room alone pays the difference, and a traveller who agrees to share but ends up alone because of an odd number may be treated differently. Decide your rule before the deposit and write it on the booking form.

Camps are smaller than hotels. A tented camp in the Mara may have only a few family tents, and a remote Botswana camp a handful of rooms, so a big group may be split across two camps of the same standard.

What Happens When Someone Drops Out or Joins Late?

When someone drops out, their cancellation charges follow our terms and conditions, and the shared costs are spread across fewer people. When someone joins late, they can usually slot in if rooms, seats and permits are still free. Both are easier with a clear rule agreed at the start.

Share the terms with every traveller before group safari payments begin, and ask each one to confirm they have read them. That single step stops most disputes.

Permits and flights booked in a name

Gorilla permits and some internal flights are booked with each traveller's passport details, so a swap is not always possible. Our guide to gorilla permits for groups in Rwanda explains how permits are sold in blocks of eight per gorilla family, and the Rwanda Development Board gorilla tracking page sets out the official rules. Check spelling against passports before anything is booked.

Why cover matters for group safari payments

Ask everyone to buy travel insurance when they pay their deposit, with cancellation cover and medical evacuation. If one member has to cancel for illness, their insurance can repay their share while the rest of the group carries on. Our page on travel insurance for safaris lists what to look for.

How Should a Group Handle Flights, Arrivals and Paperwork?

A group handles flights best by letting each member book their own and sending us every flight number once ticketed. We match transfers to each arrival, and you keep one shared file of flights, passports and insurance numbers.

Kenya needs an electronic travel authorisation for most visitors. The official Kenya eTA FAQs say each passenger needs their own eTA even in a group, that one person may apply on behalf of others, and that there is an option to apply as a group. Normal processing starts at US$30 per traveller and usually takes up to three working days (checked November 2026). Confirm the fee before you apply.

The same FAQs list a passport valid for at least six months with at least one blank page as a typical requirement (checked November 2026). Our Kenya eTA guide walks through the form, and groups visiting Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda together should read about the East Africa Tourist Visa.

Plan a gentle first day. Long-haul arrivals followed by a long drive tire everyone, so many groups add a night in Nairobi or Arusha.

Insider Tips

  • Use one form: Collect names as in passports, room-sharing, diets and flights on a single form
  • Set early deadlines: Ask members to pay a week before the real due date
  • Name a deputy: Give a second person access to the ledger and rooming list
  • Date every version: Send lodges only the latest rooming list, with the date in the file name
  • Price extras separately: Balloon flights and spa treatments are paid only by those who take them
  • Keep a waiting list: A ready replacement protects free places and shared costs

A Countdown Organisers Can Follow

The simplest way to keep group safari payments and rooms on track is a countdown with one task per stage. Pin it in your group chat.

Time before travelOrganiser task
9 to 12 monthsShare dates, a rough budget and the route; ask for a group quote
6 to 9 monthsCollect deposits and passport names; agree the free place rule
3 to 4 monthsCollect flight numbers; remind everyone about visas or eTAs
6 to 8 weeksClose the rooming list and send diets and medical notes
2 to 4 weeksBalances paid; share the itinerary and packing list
1 weekCheck every eTA or visa and insurance policy number is in the shared file

Frequently Asked Questions

How do group safari payments work with Divulge Adventures?

Group safari payments work in two stages. A deposit of 30 to 40% of each traveller's share holds the booking, and the balance is due 2 to 4 weeks before travel. Each traveller can pay their own share directly, so the organiser does not collect everyone's money.

Who gets the free place on a group safari?

The group decides who gets the free place. On our group bookings the seventh place is free for every six paying travellers. Most groups give it to the organiser, who does the unpaid admin, but some split the saving across everyone or use it for a teacher, a chaperone or a group doctor. Agree this in writing before anyone pays a deposit.

Can members of a group safari arrive on different flights?

Yes. Members of a group safari can arrive on different flights and from different cities. We match airport transfers to each arrival in Nairobi or Kilimanjaro, and many groups book a first night near the airport so that late arrivals can rest before the first long drive. Send us every flight number as soon as it is booked.

How many people share a room on safari?

On safari most rooms take two people, as a double or a twin, and many lodges have a limited number of triple and family rooms. Tented camps often have fewer triples than town hotels. Travellers who want a room to themselves usually pay a single supplement, so ask everyone about room-sharing early, before the rooming list goes to the lodges.

What happens if someone drops out of a group safari?

If someone drops out of a group safari, cancellation charges follow our terms and conditions and depend on how close to travel they cancel. The remaining travellers may also see their share change, because shared costs such as vehicles are split across fewer people. A replacement traveller can sometimes take the place, but permits and flights booked in a name may not transfer.

Final Thoughts

Clear group safari payments come down to a few decisions made early: who pays whom, who gets the free place, how rooms are shared and what happens if someone drops out. Write those rules down before the first deposit and the rest of the admin becomes routine.
